items.title: Hank Cicalo interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 30, 2022

ctx.x: I never really had that much trouble with producers wanting to do something differently. Usually the producer would say you know this particular artist doesn’t like to look in the booth. Okay, fine, so you set them up facing the studio. You’ve got to make the artist as comfortable as possible. And that was — because it made it easier for you. I can remember dates with guys would talk, artists would talk about, “I hated to go to that guy. He always put me in a dark room and I couldn’t sing and I couldn’t see the…

to look in the booth when there’s people in there. I don’t like to see the lights on.” I always worked with my lights down low once I got the balance I needed and that was it. People would look at me and say, “Gee are you guys in the booth?” “Yeah.” My thing was you get it as comfortable out there. For example with Carole King, Carole liked to work, because she was a musician, she liked to work with the band. So I had to set up those dates with a piano in the middle of the room and Carole would be there, and…
Can I ask you about “Tapestry” and did you have a feeling with that record in particular that this was going to be a hit?
